analysis.one_liner: Opens an eight-week health insurance signup window and bans out-of-pocket costs for COVID-19 treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it was introduced April 10, 2020, sent to three committees, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, the bill would have opened a special eight-week signup window on the health insurance exchanges so uninsured people could get coverage outside the usual open enrollment season, with $25 million for outreach to tell them about it. It would also have required all private health plans to cover medically necessary COVID-19 treatment — including telehealth visits — with no deductibles, copays, or coinsurance, and created a private right of action so patients could sue plans that refused. Insurers who waived those charges would be paid back dollar-for-dollar by the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and newly laid-off workers who could sign up for exchange coverage outside the normal enrollment season, and anyone with private insurance facing large deductibles and copays for COVID-19 testing, treatment, and telehealth visits. Outreach funds were targeted at hard-to-reach groups including limited-English-proficient populations and young adults.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured workers and people with high-deductible plans

how_it_helps.text: Creates a special enrollment period on the exchanges, running eight weeks on the federal exchange beginning one week after enactment, open to anyone eligible for a qualified health plan; states that had already opened their own COVID enrollment windows are exempt.
Lets people who enrolled during the window backdate coverage to April 1, 2020, or the first of the following month, so care already received could be covered.

Requires group health plans and individual insurance — including grandfathered plans — to cover medically necessary COVID-19 treatment, including telehealth visits, with no cost sharing, for people diagnosed with or presumed to have COVID-19.
Reimburses insurers dollar-for-dollar from the Treasury for the cost sharing they waive, so the federal government rather than patients absorbs the cost.

Appropriates $25 million for culturally and linguistically appropriate outreach about the enrollment window, and bars using those funds to promote short-term or association health plans that don't meet ACA standards.
Gives patients a private right of action to sue a plan or issuer that violates the no-cost-sharing requirement.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations to reimburse insurers for waived cost sharing and the $25 million outreach appropriation. Insurers bear the administrative work of tracking and reporting waived charges but are made whole financially.

drawbacks.text: The no-cost-sharing mandate applies only to people who have or are presumed to have COVID-19, so it does nothing for the routine care people were delaying during the pandemic, and the coverage guarantee lasts only as long as the federal emergency period designation.

The federal government pays insurers the full amount of waived cost sharing, which is more expensive for taxpayers than approaches that relied on insurers or providers to absorb part of the cost, and the reimbursement methodology was left entirely to agency guidance.

The special enrollment period requires enrollees to pay full premiums for exchange plans; it expands access to coverage but not necessarily to affordable coverage, since no additional premium subsidies were included.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients was real and immediate at the peak of the pandemic: free COVID treatment and a chance for the uninsured to get covered. The main honest cost is fiscal — taxpayers rather than insurers pay for the waived cost sharing — and the bill leaves key details to later agency guidance. Still, the core protections were straightforward and the reimbursement structure was designed to avoid forcing insurers to eat losses, which arguably made the bill more passable, not less.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raul Ruiz introduced the Care for COVID-19 Act 2.0 on April 10, 2020, with Rep. Lauren Underwood as its sole cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees on the day of introduction.
On April 14, 2020, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no further action of any kind was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
No committee reported the bill and no floor vote was ever scheduled in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers faced no new mandate, and the tens of millions of uninsured and underinsured Americans kept paying out of pocket for COVID testing and treatment through the rest of the emergency.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and federal inaction; patients kept paying

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in any of the three committees to which it was referred.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; no vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Declined to open a nationwide special enrollment period on the federal exchange during the 2020 pandemic, resisting calls to do so, which reduced pressure to legislate one.

sides.party_line_note: Both named supporters were Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; the bill never drew a recorded vote, so no formal party split exists.

industries.note: The bill would have forced plans to waive deductibles and copays on COVID treatment, but reimbursed them dollar-for-dollar from the Treasury, so insurers would have gained administrative burden and lost little revenue. For patients, the same arrangement meant treatment at no out-of-pocket cost, so the industry's interest did not run against the public's here.

industries.industry: Health care providers and telehealth companies
industries.note: Requiring coverage of medically necessary COVID care, explicitly including telehealth visits, with federal reimbursement of waived patient charges would have meant more bills actually paid, supporting telehealth expansion during the emergency.
